plain.text: In Thessalonica, Paul went to the synagogue as usual and for three Sabbaths reasoned from the Scriptures, explaining that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. "This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Messiah." Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and quite a few prominent women believed. But others became jealous, formed a mob and started a riot. Not finding Paul, they dragged Jason, who had welcomed them, before the city officials, shouting, "These men who have caused trouble all over the world have now come here!"

The believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. The Bereans were of more noble character than those in Thessalonica, because they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true. Many believed. When opponents came from Thessalonica to stir up trouble, the believers sent Paul to the coast and on to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind.

In Athens, Paul was greatly distressed to see that the city was full of idols. He reasoned in the synagogue and in the marketplace every day with whoever happened to be there. Some philosophers began to debate with him. Some called him a babbler; others thought he was promoting foreign gods, because he was preaching about Jesus and the resurrection. They brought him to a meeting of the Areopagus, curious about this new teaching. (The Athenians spent their time talking about the latest ideas.)

Paul said, "People of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. I even found an altar with the inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. What you worship as something unknown, I am going to proclaim to you." The God who made the world and everything in it does not live in temples built by human hands. He gives everyone life and breath. From one man he made all the nations, so that people would seek him and perhaps reach out and find him, "though he is not far from any one of us. For in him we live and move and have our being," as some of their own poets said. In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. He has set a day to judge the world by the man he appointed, and has given proof by raising him from the dead. When they heard about the resurrection, some sneered, others said, "We want to hear you again on this subject." A few became followers, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, and a woman named Damaris.

summary.bigIdea: Paul shares the good news in different ways: reasoning from Scripture in synagogues and starting from the culture in Athens.
points: In Thessalonica, many believe but a riot breaks out.
The Bereans eagerly check the Scriptures daily.
In Athens, Paul speaks about the "unknown god" who is not far from any of us.
summary.reflection: The Bereans checked what they heard against Scripture. How do you test what you hear about God?
